problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all treat motion as something that must satisfy several audiences at once. A character should follow an artist's intent, keep body parts connected, make contacts land in the right places, and still move as if weight, balance, timing, cloth, hands, muscles, or object interactions matter. The computer may receive a text prompt, a captured sequence, a sketch, a few seconds of style examples, a body with unusual proportions, a hand view, a cloth scan, or a streamable 3D video. None of those inputs is the motion itself. They are partial evidence about how something should change over time. The shared problem is to turn that evidence into a believable sequence of states: bones, surfaces, hands, strokes, texture, volume, or object parts at one moment, then the next, without losing identity or breaking contact. The family is wider than human walking. It includes non-human characters, athletic control, piano-playing hands, exaggerated bodies, layered drawings, deforming textures, deployable cut patterns, cloth capture, and long volumetric video. They are siblings because each asks how time can be generated, transferred, compressed, or cleaned while preserving the relationships that make motion readable.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would try to copy motion directly. Put the same joint angles on a new character, interpolate drawings halfway between key frames, smooth captured hands, repeat a stored motion clip, or compress each frame as if it were unrelated to the previous one. For control, they might ask a learned policy to imitate examples and hope it survives a new environment. These ideas fail because motion is relational. A footstep only looks right if it reaches the ground at the correct time and does not slide. A hand grasp only works if fingers, object, wrist, and body agree. A style is not just a pose; it is also rhythm, exaggeration, and which body region carries the change. A drawing stroke may disappear behind another layer. A new body shape can turn a valid action into self-contact or impossible balance. Treating frames independently also creates jitter, missing details, or huge storage cost.
mathematical_principle: The recurring math idea is coordinated change through time. Each method chooses a compact description of the moving thing, measures what must stay true, and then fills in or adjusts the missing motion so those truths conflict as little as possible. What is being adjusted may be a skeleton, muscle activations, body-root motion, finger bends, cloth surface points, stroke layers, soft 3D video anchors, character proportions, or movable CAD parts. What counts as wrong depends on the paper: drifting away from a reference action, breaking contact, losing self-contact after retargeting, mismatching captured cloth, producing unstable volumetric video, asking muscles to perform an incoherent command, or failing to honor a sketch's intended joint. Several papers use learning, meaning they reuse patterns seen in examples, but the useful idea is not the label. The useful idea is that examples provide a smaller space of likely motions, while constraints keep the result tied to the current body, object, camera, or timing. Other papers split motion into pieces: posture versus timing, root motion versus body detail, coarse cloth shape versus wrinkles, or old frame content versus the change from one frame to the next. The tradeoff is freedom versus consistency: enough freedom to create or adapt motion, enough consistency that the viewer believes the moving object is the same physical thing over time.
why_math_matters: The math matters because motion has structure that a single picture cannot reveal. Bodies have parts connected by joints; hands have many small controls that must act together; muscles create motion indirectly through forces; cloth and deformable surfaces carry wrinkles from nearby frames; drawings have visible and hidden layers; volumetric video contains pieces that persist while the camera sees changing surfaces. These structures make time predictable in limited ways. If a hand is touching a piano key now, the next frame should not teleport the finger away unless the action says so. If a character has longer arms, the old motion must bend around that shape instead of simply replaying old numbers. If a motion style is learned from a few seconds, the system must separate what is a stable posture preference from what is a timing pattern, or it will copy the example too literally. Anchors, constraints, losses, policies, and decompositions are bookkeeping devices for these relationships. They tell the method which differences are allowed, which differences signal a mistake, and which details can be reused from neighboring time steps or examples.
paper_family: The representative papers are different branches of the same problem: carry intent through time without breaking the moving object's internal logic. ACT starts at the broadest level by joining rigging and animation, so an unusual character can receive both a controllable body structure and motion rather than treating setup and action as separate chores. HIL, MUSIC, and ReActor focus on control: an athletic body, muscle-driven hand, or robot must imitate examples while still surviving forces, balance, and new tasks. STyMo, DMP, skinned retargeting, MotionBricks, and autoregressive human motion generation adapt or create motion under user control, but each must protect timing, contacts, body proportions, or region-specific style. MOCHI and OmniHands repair or capture interactive motion where hands, objects, and multiple people create missing data and contact mistakes. LayerInbetween solves a 2D version of the same time problem by matching strokes across frames while reasoning about occlusion and layers. The compression and anchored volumetric-video papers preserve moving 3D content by storing changes and stable time anchors instead of treating every frame as new. Cloth capture, deforming texture, kirigami deployment, and Sketch2Arti show the physical and design side: surfaces, cuts, textures, and mechanical parts need motion parameters that obey how the object can actually bend, unfold, or articulate.
what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that motion work is becoming less tied to one body type, one capture setup, or one offline authoring pipeline. The evidence emphasizes arbitrary character shapes, few-shot style examples, text and constraint control, real-time streaming, zero-shot adaptation, interactive hands, collaborative human-object motion, and long volumetric sequences. Another change is stronger coupling between generated motion and physical or contact evidence. Several papers do not merely make a plausible sequence; they refine grasps, preserve self-contact, train against physics-aware goals, track muscles, or keep cloth coherent through capture. Learned models appear often, but they are increasingly wrapped around explicit controls, anchors, decompositions, and constraints.
limits: The evidence does not prove that these methods handle every body, motion, object, or capture condition. Many depend on training data, paired style examples, reference motions, template cloth, readable sketches, known CAD structure, camera views, marker patterns, or bodies close enough to the method's assumptions. Physical controllers can still fail when contacts, terrain, strength, or timing fall outside their experience. Retargeting and generation methods may preserve some contacts while losing others. Compression and volumetric-video methods assume enough temporal coherence to exploit previous frames. The abstracts describe contributions more than failure cases, so they do not establish behavior under severe occlusion, unusual anatomy, fast hand-object interaction, extreme cloth folding, unsupported art styles, or deployment on every real-time system.
